key_insight: The paper shows that adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) cell density can act as a compact latent representation to predict spray breakup dynamics and nozzle-geometry-conditioned interface evolution.
engineering_relevance: This enables much faster spray-nozzle design exploration by replacing expensive VOF-AMR CFD runs with a surrogate that preserves key transient two-phase breakup behavior.
method: Encode AMR cell-density fields instead of full flow states.
Reconstruct transient density and nozzle geometry, then use a second stage for remaining flow variables.
evidence_signal: On held-out simulations, the surrogate captures key interface dynamics and runs in 0.045 s per trajectory, over 6×10^4 faster than Basilisk CFD.
watch_item: Because the surrogate relies on learned AMR refinement structure, performance may drop for nozzle geometries or breakup regimes outside the training distribution.
paper_title: Learning Interface Breakup: A Geometry-Conditioned Latent Surrogate for Spray Formation
